A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive-regularization work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial additions and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original AUC comparisons on iPinYou, Amazon Electronics, Avazu and LZD, plus learning curves, feature-filtering experiments and weight-decay sensitivity results.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results with three-seed averages and standard deviations, alongside frequency-bucket ablations, embedding-size experiments and singular-spectrum analyses.

M1.justification: The clipped interval-dependent regularization rule and AdamAR/AdagradAR update procedures remain unchanged. Section 3.1 clarifies time indices consistently with the existing pseudocode; moving AdagradAR from Appendix B to G does not introduce a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same tasks and four datasets: iPinYou, Amazon Electronics, Avazu and LZD. Dataset descriptions move from Section 4.1.1 to Appendix L. New frequency-bucket and architecture analyses use retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds SAM as a comparator in both Adam and Adagrad benchmark comparisons, including Tables 1–2 and the learning-curve analysis. The native optimizers, MEDA and fixed-weight-decay comparators remain, making this a focused expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported benchmark backbone changes from DeepFM to xDeepFM, supported by different citations and CIN configurations. The stated decay-search range changes from 10^-7–10^-1 to 10^n with n=-6.5,-6,...,-1. New protocols introduce progressive adaptation across five frequency buckets, embedding sizes 16–128, and singular-spectrum diagnostics. These are reported setting changes and additions; they do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 4.5 isolates frequency-dependent regularization through bucket analysis and progressive replacement of fixed decay. Appendix E adds embedding-size sensitivity and embedding-collapse diagnostics. Weight-decay sensitivity expands from Avazu alone to all four datasets in Appendix I. The original IP-filtering analysis remains.

E5.justification: V1 supplies point scores without run-count or uncertainty reporting. V2 states that Section 4.3 experiments use three different seeds, reports averages in Tables 1–2 and standard deviations in Tables 8–11, and discloses seed matching. This newly documents statistical replication; it does not establish an increase from a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace many earlier scores with reported three-seed averages; for example, Avazu/DNN/AdamAR epoch-2 AUC changes from 0.7640 to 0.7631. These are revised reported results under changed reporting/settings. SAM adds new rankings, including Amazon/WDL/Adam epoch-1 AUC of 0.8516 versus AdamAR's 0.8496. Bucket, embedding-size, spectrum and expanded sensitivity results are also added.

T1.justification: V2 adds nonconvex convergence assumptions and Proposition 3 in Section 3.3, its derivation and occurrence-interval noise bounds in Appendix B, a Clarke-subgradient treatment of nonsmooth optimality in Appendix C, and an FM-like Rademacher-complexity derivation in Appendix D. These substantially extend the original theoretical analysis.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: explaining sparse-embedding overfitting, proposing adaptive regularization, improving single- and multi-epoch performance, and production deployment. The abstract now explicitly names Rademacher complexity and norm-budget control without materially changing those claims.

C2.justification: V2 supplements the retained norm-growth explanation with an embedding-collapse interpretation, attributes high-frequency-bucket gains to larger norm budgets, and offers sparsity-dependent coefficient guidance. Section 4.3 also qualifies the performance narrative by acknowledging SAM's single-epoch advantage on Amazon.

D1.justification: V2 documents xDeepFM CIN configurations and adds analytic optimizer computation/storage costs, including AdamAR's 4P versus Adam's 3P memory requirement, excluding gradient computation. It explicitly specifies embedding-only decay for the fixed-decay baselines. The code-access URL, hardware, batch size and learning rates remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds supporting references for SAM, convergence theory, nonsmooth analysis and embedding collapse. The experimental setup cites Zhang et al. (2024) for the recommendation WuKong architecture instead of Gu et al. (2022), and the DIN citation disappears with shortened dataset discussion. The central positioning against MEDA and uniform decay remains stable.

P1.justification: V2 lightly revises the abstract and notation, condenses Section 4.1 into labeled paragraphs, moves dataset descriptions to Appendix L, and reorganizes appendix labels around added material. Most introduction, method explanation and conclusion prose remains intact; the document is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds bucket and spectrum visualizations, three additional dataset sensitivity figures, ablation/embedding-size/resource tables, and four mean-plus-standard-deviation tables. Existing benchmark tables and Figure 1 gain SAM entries. V1's Avazu sensitivity Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 7, while the feature-statistics table is retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V1 lacks reported run variability and direct component ablations of frequency adaptation. V2 addresses these important evidential gaps with three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and progressive bucket ablations, supplemented by SAM comparisons and embedding-size analyses. Acknowledging SAM's Amazon advantage also improves qualification of the findings. These substantially strengthen validation and transparency, despite minor editing defects such as Figure 1 still saying 'four methods' while displaying five.
